supported_facts: ProPublica reported that businesses tied to Trump's family and associates were approved for as much as $21 million in PPP loans.
The recipients included a lettuce-farming venture backed by Trump's son and Kushner Companies; the article concerns loan approvals, not necessarily amounts actually disbursed or forgiven.
unsupported_original_claims: The reviewed article does not establish that the Trump Organization itself received PPP assistance.
The broad claim that politically connected applicants displaced more deserving small businesses and the conflict-of-interest conclusion need distinct evidence.
access_notes: Read ProPublica's July 6, 2020 article and update; it identifies the family/associate ties and describes the figures as loan approvals/amounts to receive.
corrected_title: PPP Loan Approvals Went to Businesses Tied to Trump's Family and Associates
corrected_claim: ProPublica reported that businesses tied to members of Donald Trump's family and associates were approved for as much as $21 million in Paycheck Protection Program loans. Examples included a lettuce-farming venture backed by Trump's son and Kushner Companies. The article documents loans approved for related businesses; it does not establish that the Trump Organization itself received PPP funding or that every approved dollar was disbursed.
exact_gap: No reviewed source establishes a PPP loan to the Trump Organization itself. The broader claims about preferential access, displaced applicants and conflicts require separate, claim-specific support.

supported_facts: HHS announced on June 9, 2025 that it removed all 17 sitting members of CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and would reconstitute the committee.
The official announcement identifies ACIP's advisory role in vaccine recommendations.
unsupported_original_claims: The action did not occur on February 10, 2025.
This announcement does not substantiate the synopsis's claims about the credentials or ideology of later appointees or predictions of particular outbreaks.
access_notes: Read HHS's June 9 press release; it gives the date, the 17-member removal and agency explanation.
corrected_title: Kennedy Removes All 17 Sitting Members of CDC Vaccine Advisory Committee
corrected_claim: On June 9, 2025, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced that the department had removed all 17 sitting members of CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and would reconstitute the panel. HHS describes ACIP as advising CDC on vaccine safety, efficacy and clinical need. The announcement was in June, not February; claims about subsequent appointees and predicted health effects require separate evidence.
exact_gap: The official source supports the date and removal, but not the frozen date or assertions about the qualifications of eventual replacements and downstream disease outbreaks.

supported_facts: On May 15, 2025, Labor, HHS and Treasury said they would not enforce the portions of the 2024 MHPAEA final rule that were new compared with the 2013 rule while litigation was pending, plus an additional 18 months after a final decision.
The agencies explicitly said statutory MHPAEA obligations continued to have effect.
unsupported_original_claims: The administration did not rescind all parity protections in March 2025 or free insurers from the statute's parity requirements.
The reviewed statement does not establish the synopsis's claims about specific coverage practices, a 74-million-person abandonment, or an APA condemnation.
access_notes: Read the joint agency statement on the DOL page and its PDF; both returned the May 15 date and limited non-enforcement scope.
corrected_title: Agencies Pause Enforcement of New 2024 Mental Health Parity Rule Provisions
corrected_claim: On May 15, 2025, the Departments of Labor, HHS and Treasury said they would not enforce the provisions newly added by the 2024 Mental Health Parity final rule while related litigation was pending, plus 18 months after a final decision. The agencies stated that statutory MHPAEA obligations remained in effect. This was a limited pause concerning new rule provisions, not a repeal of mental-health parity law or a March end to all enforcement.
exact_gap: The frozen date and assertion that insurers were freed from parity obligations are inaccurate. The agency statement does not support the entry's claims about specific resulting coverage practices or affected-population figures.

supported_facts: The FY2026 Education budget request, released May 30, 2025, proposed continued Pell Grant funding but set the maximum 2026–27 Pell award at $5,710, $1,685 below the prior award maximum.
The student-aid justification proposed cutting Federal Work-Study from $1.23 billion to $250 million and eliminating the $910 million Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant appropriation.
The higher-education justification proposed zero discretionary funding for Federal TRIO programs.
unsupported_original_claims: The request did not propose eliminating all federal student aid; it retained Pell funding and requested some Work-Study funding.
The impacts predicted for community colleges, HBCUs and tribal colleges and the claimed ideological objective are not established by the budget tables alone.
The proposal was not enacted law; its requested amounts and program reductions should be described as a proposal.
access_notes: Read the official FY2026 budget request and the Department of Education's student-aid and higher-education justifications; the tables specify proposed levels and reductions.
Read Education Week's report for the May 30, 2025 release date. The official documents are budget proposals, not evidence of enacted cuts.
corrected_title: Trump's FY2026 Education Budget Proposes Pell, Work-Study and TRIO Cuts, Not an End to All Aid
corrected_claim: The administration released its FY2026 Education budget request on May 30, 2025. The proposal retained Pell Grants but lowered the proposed maximum award for 2026–27 to $5,710, proposed reducing Federal Work-Study funding from $1.23 billion to $250 million, and proposed eliminating the Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant and discretionary TRIO funding. These were proposed cuts, not enacted changes, and the budget did not eliminate all federal student aid.
exact_gap: The frozen claim overstates a set of targeted proposed cuts as complete elimination of federal aid. Budget documents do not by themselves establish the predicted effects on particular institution types or the administration's asserted long-term motive.

supported_facts: Reuters reported on January 22, 2025 that DOJ ordered its Civil Rights Division to pause ongoing litigation left from the Biden administration, pursue no new cases, and agree to no settlements while matters were reviewed.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited report does not support placing the entire division's senior leadership on leave on January 21 or effectively shutting down the division.
The source does not show that all voting-rights litigation or police consent decrees were abandoned or that the division stopped enforcing all civil-rights laws.
access_notes: Read Reuters' contemporaneous report, which describes an internal memo and a litigation pause.
corrected_title: DOJ Orders Civil Rights Division to Pause Litigation Pending Review
corrected_claim: On January 22, 2025, the Justice Department ordered its Civil Rights Division to pause ongoing Biden-era litigation, pursue no new cases and agree to no settlements while the matters were reviewed, according to an internal memo reported by Reuters. This was a litigation-review directive; the reviewed evidence does not show that the division's entire leadership was placed on leave or that the agency ceased operating.
exact_gap: The verified event is the January 22 litigation pause. The entry's January 21 leadership claim and assertions that all federal civil-rights enforcement stopped are unsupported by the reviewed source.

supported_facts: Reuters reported that Trump removed NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo on January 27, 2025.
Reuters reported that Wilcox's removal deprived the board of a quorum, leaving it unable to issue decisions; the agency spokesperson said no reason was given for the removals.
unsupported_original_claims: Trump did not fire all sitting NLRB members, and the event was not on January 20.

The source does not show that hundreds of cases were frozen indefinitely or that 100 million workers had no enforcement body; the agency's General Counsel was also removed, but that is separate from board membership.
access_notes: Read Reuters' January 28 report and its follow-up on Wilcox's lawsuit; both describe the two officials and the quorum issue.
corrected_title: Trump Fires NLRB Member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo
corrected_claim: On January 27, 2025, President Trump removed National Labor Relations Board member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo. Reuters reported that Wilcox's removal deprived the five-member board of a quorum, preventing it from issuing decisions, and that no reason for the removals was given. Trump did not fire every sitting board member, as the frozen title claims.
exact_gap: The event was two removals on January 27, not the firing of all board members on January 20. The supplied evidence supports a loss of quorum but not the broader quantified claims about all pending cases or workers' access to enforcement.

supported_facts: The Associated Press reported that on March 6, 2006, Trump and Ivanka appeared on The View; in response to a hypothetical about Playboy, he said she had a 'very nice figure' and that if she were not his daughter, perhaps he would be dating her.
The comment is from The View appearance, not the September 5 Howard Stern interview identified in the frozen title.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited quote is misattributed to the Howard Stern interview and the date is wrong.
The second quotation in the frozen synopsis is from a separate appearance and should not be blended into this discrete event.
The source does not establish a broader pattern from this one remark.
access_notes: Read the AP-sourced Today.com article and the AP-syndicated USA Today copy; both identify the March 2006 The View appearance and provide the quotation.
corrected_title: Trump Says on The View He Might Date Ivanka If She Were Not His Daughter
corrected_claim: During a March 6, 2006 appearance on The View, Donald Trump responded to a hypothetical about Ivanka posing for Playboy by saying she had a 'very nice figure' and that if she were not his daughter, perhaps he would be dating her, according to the Associated Press. This is the The View remark, not the separate Howard Stern interview named in the frozen record; other Ivanka comments belong to separate episodes.
exact_gap: The exact quote is supportable, but its venue/date in the frozen title are wrong and the synopsis combines remarks from different interviews.

supported_facts: AP reported that U.S. imports of Ivanka Trump merchandise rose an estimated 166% over the prior year while the brand's sales reached record levels.
The AP/CBS report separately documented provisional Chinese trademark approvals while Ivanka Trump was a White House adviser.
unsupported_original_claims: The 166% figure does not measure profits or sales growth.
The cited article does not establish that trademark approvals tracked policy decisions or that the administration's trade policy caused commercial growth.
access_notes: Read the AP reporting republished by CBS News; it distinguishes import estimates, revenue, sales and provisional trademarks.
corrected_title: Ivanka Trump Merchandise Imports Rise 166% as Brand Sales Reach Record Levels
corrected_claim: Associated Press reporting in April 2017 said U.S. imports of Ivanka Trump merchandise, almost all from China, rose an estimated 166% over the prior year while the brand reported record sales. Its provisional Chinese trademark approvals were a separate development while Ivanka Trump served as a White House adviser. The import statistic does not represent a 166% increase in sales or profits.
exact_gap: The source corrects the metric from sales/profits to imports. It does not establish that White House service or U.S. foreign policy caused either the import change or trademark approvals.

supported_facts: The State Department says it began requesting social-media identifiers from most immigrant and nonimmigrant visa applicants worldwide in 2019.

Reuters reported that on June 18, 2025 the State Department ordered resumed student-visa appointments with tighter online-presence screening for applicants, including those applying for F, M and J visas, and instructed applicants to make profiles public.
unsupported_original_claims: No January 20, 2025 executive order requiring all visa applicants to provide five years of social-media history was found in the reviewed sources.
The sources do not establish that applicants were denied based on protected political expression or that the policy primarily targeted Muslim-majority-country applicants.
access_notes: Read the State Department's 2019 notice and Reuters' report on the June 2025 cable; the sources establish distinct policies with different scopes and dates.
corrected_title: Trump Administration Tightens Online Vetting for Student and Exchange-Visitor Visas
corrected_claim: Social-media identifiers were already requested from most U.S. visa applicants worldwide beginning in 2019. In June 2025, the State Department directed more comprehensive online-presence screening for F, M and J student and exchange-visitor visa applicants as appointments resumed, Reuters reported. The 2025 measure had a narrower scope than the long-running identifier requirement; the reviewed sources do not support a January 20 executive order covering all visa applicants.
exact_gap: The entry conflates the 2019 identifier collection with a narrower June 2025 review. No reviewed source substantiates the claimed January 20 executive order, content-based denial mechanism or affected-group description.

supported_facts: Reuters reported that Trump announced the Stargate private-sector venture at the White House on January 21, 2025, involving OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle and a plan for up to $500 billion in AI infrastructure investment over four years.
The source describes prospective investment, not $500 billion already deployed.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited report documents an announcement of a business venture, not an executive order.
It does not establish that SoftBank received favorable regulatory treatment in exchange for the pledge.
The source does not verify Musk's separate criticism or a specific resulting rift with Sam Altman.
access_notes: Read Reuters' January 21 report; its lead describes the companies' announcement and planned investment.
corrected_title: Trump Announces Stargate AI Infrastructure Venture With Up to $500 Billion Planned Investment
corrected_claim: At the White House on January 21, 2025, Trump joined leaders from OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle to announce Stargate, a private-sector venture that planned up to $500 billion in U.S. AI infrastructure investment over four years. The amount was a prospective plan, not money already deployed. The Reuters report documents an announcement, not an executive order or a regulatory exchange for the pledge.
exact_gap: The source supports the announcement and planned investment but not the original executive-order mechanism, quid-pro-quo implication, or separate claims about Musk and Altman.
